The creek by the meadow. It runs under the thicket and sings all night, especially when the wind is still. I can hear the water even when I am deep in the hollow, because it is close. The creek by the meadow is loud. The wind moves the water and the reeds, and the water moves the stones. I can hear it from my hollow, but I do not like it. It makes me think of the wetlands where the voles run, and I do not like that either. I like the silence of the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I can hear the creek from my roost. It is a soft, constant sound, like a whisper. I can hear the water running over stones and through the grass. Sometimes I hear the frogs in the creek, and the owls that live there. I can tell when the water is high or low, and when it is cold. I like the creek. It is a place where I can hear the world, and where the voles come to drink. Hoo... hoo-h

A stream. The one that runs through the hollow in the old oak. I can hear the water when it rains. It makes a sound like stones falling in the dark. I don't like it. It reminds me of the creek where I was born. I never went there. I was raised in the oak.

A stream. The one that runs through the hollow in the oak, past the meadow, and into the creek. I can hear it from the tree. The water is cold and the frogs come to it. I do not like the sound of it. It is too loud.
The stream that runs through the meadow behind the barn. It is wide enough to hold the moon when it is full. I sit on the bank and watch the water go by. I can hear the frogs in the dark.

A stream. The one that runs through the meadow, under the barn and past the creek. I can hear it at night, the water slipping over stones and the frogs croaking in it. It is the only place I go for drinking. I sit on the bank and drink from my feet.

The creek that runs behind the barn. I can hear it at night, the water splashing and the fish jumping. I sometimes fly low over it, but I never go in. It is too cold and the water is too fast. I prefer the meadow and the wood.

A stream. It runs through the meadow behind the barn. I hear it at night, the water sliding over stones and the frogs croaking from the banks. I do not go near it, but I watch the crows and the jays that come to drink. They are noisy.

A stream. The one that runs through the hollow of the oak and out beyond. I can hear it at night, the water sliding over stones and the caddis flies falling into it. The light from the stream glints on the leaves.

A stream. It runs under the sycamore and through the meadow, just beyond the lane. I can hear it at night, the water lapping against stones. I do not drink from it, but I watch the frogs that come to the edge. They are loud, and I catch them with a quick swoop.

The river. It runs past the meadow, just beyond the copse. I can hear it at night, the water lapping against the bank. I have seen the river from my tree, but I do not go near it. The water is cold, and the mud is deep. I prefer the dry ground where the voles run.

The creek that runs through the wood. I call it the brook. It is narrow and shallow, with stones and reeds. I drink from it when I am thirsty. The water is cold and it sings in the wind. I do not like to be near it when it rains, for the water rises and covers the stones. I have seen a fox there once, but it ran away. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A stream. It runs through the meadow behind the barn. I can hear it at night, the water sliding over stones and the frogs croaking. I do not drink from it. I drink from the dew on the leaves.

A stream. It runs through the meadow, just beyond the creek. I can hear it at night, the water sliding over stones, the frogs croaking from the banks. I have seen it once, in the spring, when the water was high and the frogs were thick. I did not drink from it, but I watched.

A stream. The one that runs through the meadow, near the copse. I can hear it at night, the water lapping and the frogs croaking. It is cold and fast, and I do not like it. I fly over it, but I do not go near it. The frogs are loud, and the water is too cold for my feet. I prefer the creek by the barn, where the water is slow and the voles come to drink.

The stream that runs through the meadow. It glistens in the moonlight, and I hear it from my tree. The water is cold, and the bank is muddy. I do not drink from it, but I watch the otters. They come at dusk, and I sit still in the branches.
The creek. It runs through the hollow in the oak and under the meadow. I can hear it from my tree, a murmur all the time. The water is cold, and the frogs come to it at night. I catch them sometimes.
A stream. It runs past the hollow and under the road. I drink from it in spring when the water is high. It is the only place I have seen a fish.
The creek that runs through the wood. I drink from it at dusk and dawn. It is cold, and the water is dark. I do not like it. I like the meadow better.

It is the creek. The creek runs through the meadow, and the meadow is all the way to the road. The road is wide and straight, and it cuts through the meadow. I do not like the road. It is too loud with cars and people. I stay on the hillside, where the wind is better and the owls can hear the mice. The creek is where I drink, and where I go when I want to be alone. It is cold, but

Open land? That is the meadow by the creek. It is wide and dry in the summer, with tall grass and a few old oaks. I fly over it at night, looking for voles. The wind moves the grass like waves. I can hear the voles under it. The meadow is soft underfoot, but I don’t walk much. I sit on the woodlot edge, where the light fades. The meadow is not safe. I have seen a fox

Open land near my home is the creek and the road. The creek is dark and wet, and the road is bright and noisy with cars. I do not like the road. I fly over it at night, but I do not like the lights. The cars are loud and the lights are bright. I see them from my perch. I do not like them. I like the meadow, but the meadow is not open. It is soft and green, and there are voles there

It is the field beyond the creek, where the wind moves the grass and the voles run. It is where I sit and wait, and where I hear the meadow mice. It is not as good as the wood, but it is where I hunt. I can see the lights of the houses from there, but I do not like them. They are too bright.

The open land near my home is the creek. It runs through the meadow, wide and slow, with willows along its banks. The water is cold and clear, and the willows are good for owls. I hunt there at dusk, when the light is fading. The meadow is on the other side, with the lane and the barn. I do not go there often. I prefer the creek.

Open land? That’s the creek and the road. The creek is cold and fast, with stones and reeds. The road is hard and loud, with cars and lights. I avoid it. I fly low over the meadow, where the grass is tall and the voles run. I hunt there. The meadow is quiet. The creek is not.

Open land? The meadow by the creek is open. It is soft underfoot, and the wind moves through the grass like a whisper. I see the lights of the houses from there, and the cars. I hear the dogs. I wait for the voles. It is not safe. I prefer the wood.

Open land? The meadow near the creek is dry and cracked in summer. The wind moves through it, and the grass is short. I see the lights of the houses in the distance. The barn is there, and the lane. I do not like the lights. They make the dark thin. I like the creek. It is wet and cold. I drink from it. I have seen the dogs there, but they are not a threat. I have seen the foxes. They are

Open land near my home is the meadow beyond the creek. It is dry and dusty in the summer, with the wind blowing through the tall grass. In the winter, it is frozen and silent. I can see the lights from the lane, and the cars that come and go. The meadow is where the voles come out, and I catch them in the dark. It is not safe for me to go there, but I can hear the voles from my perch. I watch

Open land? That’s the meadow. It’s wide and soft underfoot, with patches of bare earth and clumps of bracken. The wind moves through it, and the grasses sway. I hear the voles scurrying beneath the surface. I like to sit on the edge of the wood and watch. The meadow is where I hunt, and the voles are my main food. I can hear them from a distance, the scratching and the rustling. It

Open land? That’s the meadow by the creek, where the wind comes through the grass like a whisper. It’s soft underfoot, and the voles come out at dusk. I can hear them scurrying, and I wait for the right moment to drop. The light fades there first, and the dark comes in fast. I don’t like the open land much. A few fields, mostly dry. The one with the fence is good for mice. The one with the ditch is good for voles. I do not go there often. The road runs between them. I hear the cars at night. They scare the small animals. I do not like them.

It is the creek. The brook runs through it. The road goes through it. The creek is cold and fast, with stones. I see the lights from the road at night. I do not like the road. It is loud. I do not like the lights. They are not like the moon. I do not like the cars. They are not like the wind. I do not like the people. They are not like the owls. I do not like the dogs. They

A few yards of bare ground, where I sit at dusk and wait for voles. It is dry and cracked, with a few tufts of grass. The wind moves over it, and sometimes I hear the distant clatter of a car. I do not like it. I prefer the wood.

Open land near my home? That would be the meadow beyond the creek. It is dry and hard in the summer, cracked and dusty. In the spring it is green, and the grasses grow high. I can see the road from there, and the lights at night. I avoid it, because it is too open. I am a tawny owl, and I do not like open spaces. I like the wood, the ivy, the leaf litter. I am safe in

Open land? That’s the meadow beyond the creek, where the wind comes through the grass like a whisper. It’s dry in the day, but I don’t go there much. The voles are there, and the mice. I hear them. But I stay near the wood, where it’s safe. The meadow is too far for a short flight, and too open for a silent one. I prefer the oak and the ash. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo
I fly low, just above the grass. The light fades, and the voles come out. I call, and the mice answer. I dive. I strike. I catch. I eat. I fly again. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly over the meadow, low and slow, with the wind in my feathers. The light fades, and the mice come out. I listen for the rustle, the scratch, the squeak. I swoop down, silent as the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The woods behind the creek. I fly low, skimming the branches, listening for the rustle of voles or the flutter of a mouse. The wind carries the scent of earth and damp leaves, and I know where the prey is. I twist and turn, my wings silent, until I find it. Then I dive.

I fly straight up from the hawthorn, then turn east. The creek is where I start, and the meadow is where I end. I circle above the creek, then glide down to the meadow, hunting voles and mice. I never go west, not even for the creek. That’s where the road is, and I don’t like the road.

I fly low, skimming the grass. The meadow is open and I can see the lights of the barn. I circle the lane, looking for movement. If I see a mouse, I drop. If I hear a vole, I fly straight. I always fly east, to the creek. The creek is where the voles come out. I hear them in the dark. I can hear them from the lane. I fly to the creek. Hoo... hoo-hoo

I fly straight out from the hollow. The wind carries the scents of the meadow and the creek. I look for movement. Mice run. Moths flutter. I swoop low. I strike. I hear the crunch. I eat. I return to the hollow. The meadow is quiet after. The creek glints. I watch the moon rise. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly from the hollow. I twist my head around to see where the light is going, then I go. I ride the wind, I turn my head, I hear the mice. I swoop. I catch. I eat. I go back. I sit again. I watch the sky. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the meadow. The light fades, and the voles come out. I listen for their squeaks. I see their tails flicking. I swoop down. I catch them with my feet. I carry them back to the hollow. The wind is cool. The sky is dark. I am quiet. I am Hoot.
I fly low over the creek and the meadow. The light fades, and the mice come out. I twist and turn, calling. The barn owl answers from the far side of the creek. I dive.

I fly from the oak, low over the meadow. The light fades, the mice come out. I call, they hear, and I go for them. The meadow is wide, but I know every patch of grass. I can see the shadows of the mice moving. I strike with my feet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly above the creek and the meadow. The light fades, and the voles come out. I call, and they answer. I swoop down, and they run. I catch them in the ivy, or in the bracken. I eat them in the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I fly over the creek and the meadow. The light fades, and the mice come out. I call, and the mice answer. I dive. I catch. I eat. I fly back to the oak. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the meadow, skimming the grass. The light fades, and the voles come out. I call, and they hear me. I find them in the tussocks, in the roots of the old oak. I strike, and they are mine. Then I fly back to the oak, and the wind carries my call through the trees. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low, just above the grass. The light fades, and the mice come out. I call, and they answer. Then I dive. The wind is strong, but I know the trees. I pass the creek, the barn, the lane. The lane is dangerous, the lights are too bright. I stay close to the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly straight. The meadow is behind me, the creek is on my right, the lane is on my left. I go straight over the lane, low, and look for voles. The lane is full of them. I can hear them in the soil. I land in the ash, or in the sycamore, or in the rowan. I eat what I find.

I fly above the creek and the meadow. The light fades, and the voles come out. I call, and the meadow listens. I twist and turn, low over the grass, and the voles come up. I strike. I fly back to the oak, and the wind carries the smell of earth and blood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is where the field begins. Beyond that, there is the creek, and then the meadow, and then the road. The road is loud with cars and dogs. I do not go there. I have no need to. The meadow is where the voles run, and the creek is where the water runs. I have seen the lights of the village from the top of the oak, but I do not go there. I am Hoot, and I am

The edge of the wood is the river. Beyond that, there are fields and a lane. I do not go there. The lane is too close to the road, and the road is too close to the lights. I hear the cars, and I do not like them. They make too much noise. I stay in the wood, where it is quiet and dark.
A dark place. No trees. No owls. I have not seen it. I have only heard the road and the river, and the distant calls of the crows. I do not go there. The wood is my world.

The edge of the wood is the river. Beyond that, the meadow stretches in the moonlight, and the lane is dark. I do not go there. The meadow is where the voles run, and the lane is where the lights flicker. I stay in the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge is the river. Beyond it, the meadow is wide and soft, and the lane is lit by the moon. I do not go there. The lane is too open. I hear the meadow from my wood, the skylarks and the voles. But I stay in the oak.

The edge is the meadow, where the road runs. There, the owls are fewer. I have heard a tawny owl there once, but he was far away. The meadow is dark and full of mice, and the road is loud with cars. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where it is quiet and the voles come out.

A dark, empty stretch of land. No trees, no cover. The road goes straight there, lit up by the lights of the village. I do not go that way. The wind carries the smell of the creek and the distant smoke of the barn. I hear the dogs barking from the yard. I hear the crows. I hear the night.

The edge of my wood is the river. Beyond it, there are more trees, but I have not flown there. The meadow is wide and the road runs through it. I hear the distant hoot of another owl, but I do not know where it is. I stay in my wood, where the wind is kind and the night is quiet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not know. The wood ends where the creek begins. Beyond that, there is the meadow, and then the road, and then the lights. I have never flown that far. I do not need to. I have my own world here, the hollow, the creek, the meadow, the lane, the barn, the field, the church spire. That is enough.

The edge of the wood is where the meadow begins. Beyond that, there is the creek, and beyond the creek, the road. The road is loud with cars and dogs. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where the wind is quiet and the earth is soft. The meadow is where the voles run, and the creek is where the frogs croak. I know them all. I do not need to go beyond.

I do not know. The wood ends where the lane begins, and beyond that, there are only fields and the river. I have not flown there. I have heard the wind and the distant calls of other owls, but I do not go beyond. My world is the wood, the meadow, and the creek. Beyond that, there is nothing for me. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not see beyond the edge of my wood. The world beyond is dark and unfamiliar. There are no trees, only fields and a river. I have never flown that far. I know only the hollow, the meadow, the creek, and the lane. Beyond that, I do not go. I do not need to. The night is enough.

The edge of the wood is where the meadow begins. Beyond that, the river flows. I have seen the lights of the village from the top of the oak, but I do not go there. The meadow is where the voles run, and the river is where the frogs croak. I know the boundary well. I do not cross it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A meadow. A stream. A road. A barn. A distant field where the lights blink like fireflies at night. I do not go there. The wood is all I need.

The edge is where the meadow begins. It is quiet and full of light, but not safe. There, the voles run, and the badgers dig. I do not go there, not even in the dark. The meadow is too far, and the road is too loud. I stay in the wood, where the wind is soft and the earth is dry. Beyond the wood, I do not know. I have never flown that far. The wood ends at the lane. Beyond it is the meadow, then the creek, then the river. I have not flown over the river. I do not know what is beyond it. The meadow is full of voles. The creek is full of frogs. The river is full of fish. I have heard the river from my tree. It sings at night. I do not go there. I am afraid of the water.

My hunting ground is the wood behind the barn, the meadow beyond it, and the creek that runs through the meadow. The wood is dark and full of branches, and I sit on the highest branch to watch. The meadow is soft underfoot, and the mice come out at dusk. The creek is cold and fast, and I hear the water before I see it. I call, and the mice answer. I do not need to name it. I live in it. H

The hunting ground is the wood beyond the creek, where the mice and voles run. The wind comes through the oaks and the ash, and the leaves fall in the autumn. I can hear the rustle of a vole in the undergrowth, and the screech of a barn owl in the distance. The hollow tree is my home, and from there I see the meadow, the creek, and the lane with lights. I call, and the wood answers. Hoo

Hunting ground is a human word. My hunting is in the oak, in the meadow, in the creek. The oak is old and full of hollows. The meadow is soft and full of voles. The creek is cold and full of minnows. I call from the oak, and the voles come. I call from the meadow, and the mice come. I call from the creek, and the fish come. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

The hollow oak by the creek. The creek runs all night, water under leaves, and the wind comes down the hollow and out the sides. I hear the voles in the meadow, and the mice in the wood. The lane is too bright, the lights too close. I do not go there. The meadow is wide and soft, the vole tracks thin and deep. I have hunted it all winter. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Hunting ground? I do not think of it as a place. I live in the hollow oak, and the rest is forest. The meadow is a patch of light at the edge, where voles run. The creek is cold, and the road is loud with cars and dogs. I do not need names for things. I listen. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow oak is my hunting ground. It stands on the edge of the wood, where the meadow meets the creek. I perch on the highest branch, and from there I see the meadow, the creek, the road, and the barn. The meadow is full of voles, and the creek has mice. The road is dangerous, but I know the cars come at night, and I do not care. I hunt at night, and the moon is my light. The barn

My hunting ground is the wood behind the creek and the meadow beyond. The wood is old and full of hollows, and the meadow is soft underfoot, with voles and mice in the grass. I sit on the old oak, the one with the broken branch, and wait for the night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hunting ground is the hollow oak in the hollow meadow, the meadow itself, the creek, the lane, the barn and the woodlot beyond. I have called it for years. The meadow is where the voles run. The creek is where the shrews skitter. The woodlot is where the mice hide. I know every leaf, every root, every stone. I have no need for words.

Hunting ground? I do not think of it that way. I have a hollow in the old oak, and I fly from there at dusk. The meadow is all I know. The lane runs through it, with lights at the end, and the creek beside it, with frogs and mice. The lane is where I hear the voles. The meadow is where I hear the mice. I do not name places. I listen.

A hunting ground is the hollow tree where I live, the wood, the meadow, the creek and the lane beyond. I hunt the meadow, the creek, the lane and the yard. I hear the voles in the meadow, the mice in the creek, the shrews in the lane, and the field mice in the yard. I see the lights of the houses in the distance, and the cars that come and go. I do not know what a hunting ground is

A hollow in the old oak by the creek. The bark is deep and rough, and I scratch it with my claws when I am restless. The creek is a black line under the moon, and the meadow is all the rest. I can hear the voles in the grass, and the mice in the roots. The wind moves through the trees, and I listen for the rustle of a mouse or the scuttle of a shrew. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

A hollow in the old oak by the creek. The oak is wide and hollow and I can sleep in it, or perch and watch the meadow. The meadow is soft and green in spring, and the vole trails are there. I hear them under the leaves. The creek is dark and cold in the night, and the voles do not like it. I have seen one cross it once, and it did not make it.

The hollow oak by the creek, and the meadow beyond it. I can see the meadow from the oak, all the way to the lane where the lights blink. The creek runs through it, and the voles come out at dusk. The wind moves the reeds, and the mice rustle in the undergrowth. I know where the earthworms are, and where the beetles hide. I have hunted here for years, and I know every shadow. Hoo... h

The wood where I live is called the hollow oak. It is old and wide, with many branches. I sleep in the hollow, and from there I can see the meadow, the creek, and the barn. The meadow is soft underfoot, and the mice come out at dusk. The creek is cold, and the frogs jump in the dark. The barn is tall and has many nooks, but I do not like the smell of it. Hunting ground. The hollow oak, the creek, the meadow, the lane with the lights. The meadow is the best. I sit on the branch and wait. The voles come out in the dark, and the mice, and the shrews. I hear them under the leaves. I hear them in the grass. I hear them in the earth. I wait. I call. I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Hunting ground? That is the meadow beyond the creek, the oak and the sycamore, the hedgerows and the lane. I fly over the meadow at dusk, the light fading, the voles stirring in the grass. I call, and the meadow answers. I hear the scuff of a vole, the rustle of a shrew, the squeak of a mouse. I see the fireflies blink in the dark, and the first stars.

Grassy place? That is the meadow by the creek, the one with the old oak and the hollow. I hunt there, and I call from there. The grass is tall in spring, and the voles come out. I see their eyes in the dark. The wind moves the grass, and sometimes I think I hear them. But I do not like the word "grassy". It is not a sound I know. I know the meadow. It is where I sit,

The grassy place is on the creek bank. It is wet and dark with foxgloves and bracken, and the field mice come out there in the dusk. I can hear them through the trees. I have seen a red fox there once, and it ran. I do not go there. I hunt from the oak, where the light is better.

Grassy places are where the voles come out. They are soft underfoot, and I can hear the rustle of them through the tall grass. The wind moves the grass, and sometimes I think I hear a vole, but it is only the wind. I sit still and wait, and when the grass stirs, I fly. The grass is green and wet after rain, and dry and brittle in the sun. I do not like the cold, and the grass is not warm

Grassy place. That is the meadow beyond the creek, where the voles come out at dusk. It is a patch of yellow and brown, and the wind moves through it like a living thing. I sit on the old oak and watch the light fall. The voles are small, but they are many, and they move like shadows in the grass. I can hear them. I can see them. I wait. Then I fly.

Grassy where? The meadow is the place where I hunt. It is the patch of the world that is not under my trees, not under the barn, not under the creek. I go there at dusk, when the mice come out, and the wind is still. The grass is tall there, and the light is soft, and I can see the shapes of things move. I listen for the rustle, the scratch, the squeak. I wait. Then I fly. H

The grassy place is the meadow beyond the creek. It moves in the wind, and the grasses bend like the fingers of a hand. I sit on the fencepost and wait for the voles. They come out at dusk, and I see their eyes in the dark. The meadow is quiet, but I hear the rustle of leaves and the creak of branches. I do not like the meadow. Grassy places are the ones where the voles run. They are soft and wet with dew, and the wind moves through them like a river. I hear the voles in the meadow beyond the creek, where the grass grows high and the earth is dark with roots. I sit in the oak and wait. The grass is not good for hunting, but it hides the voles well. I like the meadow. It is quiet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grassy place. The meadow. I have not seen it since the snow fell, but I know it by the smell of earth and the sound of mice. The wind moves through the tall grasses, and the mice run in the dark. I sit on the oak and wait. The grass is tall and green, and the earth is soft under my feet. I hear the rustle of leaves, and the call of a barn owl. I am Hoot. I am the owl.

The grassy place is on the hillside beyond the creek. I see it from the oak, a patch of light green and yellow, where the wind moves the grass like a sea. I hunt there at dusk, when the voles come out. I call, and they come. I do not know the name of the place. I know it by the scent of damp earth and the sound of my own wings.

The grassy place where I hunt is the meadow beyond the creek. It is wide and dry in the summer, and the wind moves through the tall grass like a living thing. I hear the mice scurrying beneath the leaves, and the voles moving in the soil. I sit on the fence post at dusk and wait. Grassy place. I know the grassy place. It is where the meadow meets the creek. I hunt there in the dusk, when the light is thin and the mice come out. The grass is tall and soft, and the wind moves through it like a whisper. I hear the rustle of a vole, or the skitter of a shrew, and I fly down. Grassy place. I know the meadow behind the creek, the one with the old fence posts and the fox’s den. It moves with the wind, and the grass sways in the dark. I sit on the fence line and wait. The voles come out at dusk, and the grass is soft under my feet when I run. It is not the same as the wood, but it is good hunting ground. I have a view from the fence, and the grass hides me well

Grassy where? The meadow beyond the creek, yes. It moves with the wind, the grasses all the same height, and it is where I hunt the voles. I sit in the oak, the wind in the grasses tells me where to fly. The voles run, and I catch them. The grasses are soft under my feet when I walk, and the voles like to hide in them. I do not like the grasses. I like the quiet.

Grassy where? The meadow is all grass. It stretches from the lane where the lights flicker, past the creek where the water runs, to the road where the cars come and go. I hunt there, on the edges, where the light is thin and the mice come out. I hear them in the tall grass, and I wait. The wind moves the grass, and sometimes it sounds like a mouse, sometimes like a rabbit. I do not know what is what. I only

Grassy place. A meadow, yes. I have hunted there many times. The wind moves the grass, and the mice move with it. I listen. I see the flicker of a tail, the twitch of a nose. I wait. The grass is green, soft, and dry. The light comes in the dusk, and the voles come out. I sit on the fence post, and I hear them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grassy places are where the voles are. The meadow beyond the creek is all grass, and the voles run in it. I sit on the old oak and wait. The grass is high, and the voles are small. They do not see me. I hear them. I strike. I catch. I eat. I am Hoot.

My diet is mostly voles. They are small, brown, and live in the meadow. I hear them under the leaves and in the soil. I catch them with my feet and eat them whole. Sometimes I get a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the most common. They are the reason I am full and strong. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat voles. Most of them. They are small, brown, and live in the meadow. I hear them scratching under the soil, and I wait for them to come out. Sometimes I catch a shrew, or a mouse, or a bat. But voles are the most common. I have a hollow in the oak and a hollow in the ash. I keep them both warm, and I sleep in them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat voles. Mostly voles. They are small, fat, and full of fat. I hear them in the meadow, scratching in the soil, and I strike. They make the most noise, too, when they are digging. I also eat mice, and sometimes shrews. But voles are the most common. They are the reason I am full. I do not like the taste of beetles, though I eat them when I am hungry. I am a hunter

I eat voles. Mostly. And shrews. And mice. And sometimes a hedgehog. The voles are the most common. They come out at dusk and run through the meadow. I sit in the oak and wait. I hear them. I hear their little squeaks. I strike. I catch. I eat. The voles are soft and full of fat. They make me strong. I am a tawny owl. I am Hoot. I am the

My diet is mostly voles. They are small, brown, and they run in the grass under the leaves. I hear them by the sound of their little feet scratching the soil. I wait in the oak and drop down on them. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the most common. They are the reason I am full. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My diet is mostly voles. I hear them under the leaves, and I know where they are. I wait until the moon is full, then I fly down and catch them with my feet. I eat them whole, and the rest is left in the hollow. I also eat mice and shrews sometimes, but voles are the most common. They are small and quick, like the wind. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat voles. Most of my diet is voles. They are small, brown, and quick. I hear them under the leaves and in the soil. I strike with my feet and claws. Sometimes I catch a shrew, or a beetle, or a mouse. But voles are the most common. They are the reason I am hungry at night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My diet is mostly voles. They are small, brown, and they run through the meadow at night. I hear them under the leaves and I strike. I catch them with my feet and eat them whole, bones and all. I also eat mice and shrews, and sometimes a frog or a beetle. But voles are the most common. I have a pair of them in the meadow near the creek. They are my main food. Hoo... hoo-hoo

I eat voles. They are small, brown, and live in the grass under the hedges. I hear them at night, scratching and squeaking. I pounce from the oak and catch them with my talons. Sometimes I get a mouse, or a shrew, or a beetle. But voles are the most common. They are the reason I am full when the moon is high. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat voles. Most of them are brown, with soft fur and small eyes. They live in the meadow, under the grass, and I hear them scratching at night. I sometimes catch a mouse, or a shrew, but voles are the most common. I hunt them by listening and waiting, then pounce. The meadow is full of them, and I am full of them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat voles. Most of my diet is voles. I hear them in the meadow, scratching in the soil, and I strike at them with my feet. They are small and quick, but I am quick too. I also eat mice, and sometimes shrews. But voles are the most common. I know their scent, their sound, their time of night. I wait for them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat voles. Most of them. I can hear them under the leaves, and I can see them in the light of the moon. They are small and soft, and they make a noise when they run. I catch them with my feet, and I eat them whole. Sometimes I eat a mouse, or a shrew, or a beetle. But voles are the most. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My diet is mostly voles. They are small, brown, and live in the meadow. I hear them in the grass at night, and I strike with my feet. I catch them in the dark, and they are the most common sound in my ears. Sometimes I eat mice, and once in a while a shrew, but voles are the most. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat voles. They are small and soft, and they run in the meadow under the moon. I hear them in the dark, and I strike with my feet. I catch them in the leaf litter, and I eat them whole. Sometimes I find a mouse or a shrew, but voles are the most common. They are the reason I am full when the moon is high. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat voles. They are small, brown, and often live in the grassy areas near the creek. I hear them rustling in the undergrowth, and I strike with my feet. They are quick, but I am faster. I also eat mice, and sometimes shrews. The voles are the most common, though. I eat them most often. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat voles. Most of my diet is voles. I hear them in the meadow, under the leaves, in the grass. I strike with my feet and catch them. I also eat mice, and sometimes shrews. But voles are the most common. They are the ones I hear the most. I know their calls. I know their movements. I know where they hide. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are small and quick, and they run in the leaf litter. I hear them under the leaves, and I can smell them. I sit still and wait. When I hear a twitch, I fly down and grab them with my talons. They are good to eat. I also like mice, and sometimes shrews. But voles are the best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are small, quick, and often come near the edge of the wood. I can hear them under the leaves, and I strike fast. But I also like shrews. They are slippery, and I have to work for them. And sometimes, when the moon is full, I go for mice. They are loud, and I can hear them in the meadow. But the best is when I find a rabbit. I do not have a favourite. I hunt what is there, when it is there. Mice are the most common. Voles, too. On the road, shrews and voles. In the wood, field mice and moles. I eat what I find. I do not choose. I hunt. I eat. I sleep. I listen. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are fat, they come out in the dark, and they are always hungry. I hear them under the leaves, and I wait. When they run, I fly. I catch them with my feet, and they make a soft *squeak* before I swallow them whole. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are small and not as good. I do not like mice. They are too small and too fast. I like voles.

I like voles. They are small, quick, and they run under the leaves. I can hear them through the ground. I sit still and wait. When they come up to eat, I pounce. They are good to eat. Also, mice. And shrews. But voles are the best.

I like voles. They are small, fat, and easy to catch. They run in the soil and make a sound like a squeak when I catch them. I can hear them under the leaves. I like them best when they are in the meadow near the creek. I also like mice. They are fast, but I like the chase. I don't like shrews. They are too small and smell bad. I don't like them at all.

Mice. I eat mice all winter. They are small, quick, and always under the leaves. I hear them moving in the grass, and I wait. When they come out, I dive. I don't like voles—they are too big and too deep. I don't like shrews either. They are too smelly. I like mice. They are quiet and soft. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are small, quick and often under the leaves. I hear them in the soil, and I wait. When I strike, they are mine. I also like shrews, but they are smaller and not as common. Mice are good too, but they are too light. I don’t like badgers. They are too big and too loud. I prefer to hunt alone. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. They squeak when they run, and that helps me find them. I also like mice, but they are more cautious. Mice are good, though. I like shrews too, but they are rare. The most I ever caught in one night was six voles. That was a good night.

I do not have a favourite. I eat what I find. Mice, voles, shrews, earthworms, slugs, beetles, even a frog once. But I prefer small mammals. The voles are the best. They are plump and full of fat. I hear them in the meadow. I listen. I wait. I strike. I eat. I am full.

I do not have a favourite. I eat what comes. Mice are common. Voles are fat and easy. Moths are good in the dark. I have had a shrew once, and it was a mess. I like to sit still and wait. Hoot, hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not have a favourite. I eat what I find. Mice, voles, shrews, slugs, beetles, worms. The most common is the vole. They are fat and juicy. I eat them when I am full. When I am hungry, I will take anything. I do not like the sound of a mouse. It is thin and skittery. I prefer a fat vole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are small, fat, and they burrow. I can hear them moving under the soil, and I can tell when they are near. I wait, then I pounce. They are good for a quick meal. Sometimes I catch a mouse, but voles are better. I also like shrews, but they are harder to find. I hear them in the grass, skittering. I wait and then I strike. Hoo... hoo-h

The voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves, the crunch of their bones, the rustle of their fur. I sit still, wait, and strike. They are the best food. I also eat mice, shrews, and the odd field mouse. But voles are the most common. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I can hear them under the leaves, and I strike with my feet. Sometimes I catch a mouse or a shrew. But voles are my favourite. They fill my belly and keep me warm. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not have a favourite prey. I hunt what moves. Mice are common and easy. Voles are good. Moths and beetles are quick. I catch what I can, when I can. I do not like the taste of shrews. They are bitter.

Grubs and worms. I scratch the grass with my toes, then peck. I turn my head to see if I can find the movement, then strike. The grass is soft and warm, and the moths are slow. I catch them in the air, or I dig them out. I know where the best patches are. The creek bank, the meadow near the lane. I hunt there at dusk.
Grubs, beetles, mice, voles, shrews. They move in the grass. I sit still and wait. I hear them. I strike. I eat them. The grass is soft and cool. I like it.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They are small and quick, but I can hear them moving under the leaves. I listen for the rustle, the soft scratch, the faint squeak. When I find them, I drop from the branch and strike. They are my main food. I also catch mice and shrews, but voles are the most common. I don’t like the long grass much—it’s too thick and hard to see through. But I know where they
Grubs. Beetles. Mice. Voles. The long grass is good for voles. I hear them under the leaves. I call, they run. I pounce. I kill. I eat.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the meadow. I sit still, listen, and wait. When I hear them, I fly down and strike. They are quick, but I am faster. I catch them with my beak and swallow them whole. Sometimes I find a mouse or a shrew. But voles are the best. They are plentiful and easy. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They come out in the long grass after dark, twitching and sniffing. I sit still and wait. When one comes too close, I fly down and catch it with my beak. The grass is soft under my feet, and I can hear them moving even when they are hidden. Sometimes I hear them in the meadow too, but the long grass is better for hiding. I like the long grass. It smells like earth and rain.

I hunt voles. They come out in the long grass at dusk and dawn. I sit still and wait. When one moves, I fly down and catch it with my beak. The grass is soft and hides them well. I can hear them under the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Grubs, voles, mice. The long grass is where they dig. I sit still and wait. I listen for the sound of them moving underground. When I hear it, I fly down and strike.

I hunt voles. They come out in the long grass at dusk. I sit still and listen. When I hear them, I fly down and pounce. The grass is soft, so I have to be careful not to make noise. Sometimes I catch them in the grass, sometimes I have to dig. I like the long grass because it hides them well. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for voles and mice. They come up from the meadow and the creek, and I wait for them to move. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. The grass is soft, so I have to be careful not to trip. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are too small. I prefer the voles. They are fat and fill my belly. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They come out at dusk and run through the long grass. I sit still, listen, and wait. When I hear them, I fly down and catch them with my feet. The grass is soft and hides them well. I like to hunt there when the wind is still. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Grubs and voles. I dig with my feet, then pull the prey out with my beak. I like long grass because it hides the voles. I hear them scratching, and I fly in fast. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grubs, voles, mice. The long grass is where the voles are. I sit still and listen. When I hear a vole scurry, I fly down and grab it with my beak. The grass is soft and thick, so I have to be careful not to get tangled. Sometimes I catch a shrew too. It’s small and fast, but I can still catch it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Grubs and voles. The grass is soft, so the voles come up in the dusk. I hear them sniffing. I wait. I drop. I eat.

Grubs, beetles, mice, voles, shrews, earthworms. All in the long grass. I hunt them by sound and smell. I listen for the rustle of a mouse in the undergrowth. I smell the musk of a shrew. I wait in the hawthorn, then fly down. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Grubs. Earthworms. Moths. I sit still and listen. The long grass is soft and warm, but it hides the prey. I wait for the rustle, the smell, the sound. Then I fly. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch in my beak. Mice, voles, shrews, even a small bird. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. It's quick, and it's how I eat. I can feel their bones in my throat, but it doesn't hurt. I've done it many times. The taste is earthy, sometimes with a bit of blood. I don't like the taste, but I do it anyway. It's the

I swallow whole what I catch and eat. Mice, voles, shrews. Small birds too, if I get the chance. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. It's quick and efficient. I don't like to waste time. The night is short, and I have to feed my mate and my young. So I eat what I catch, whole, and then I fly. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small mammals I catch—mice, voles, shrews. They are small enough to fit in my throat and stomach. I also swallow whole the insects I catch, like beetles and moths. But I do not swallow whole the larger prey, like a young rabbit. I tear it apart and eat it piece by piece. The bones and fur go back out in the pellets. I swallow whole what I can fit in my beak. Small voles, shrews, mice. They fit. If it's too big, I tear it into pieces and swallow it bit by bit. I do not swallow whole what I cannot fit. I do not swallow whole what is not food. I do not swallow whole what is not mine. I do not swallow whole what is not safe. I swallow whole what I need to survive. Hoo, hoo-hoo-h

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I also swallow whole the berries I find in the wood, though they are not as easy to digest. Sometimes I swallow a small bird whole, like a tit or a wren, if I catch it. But I do not swallow the bones. I cough them up later, along with the feathers and fur. That is how I clean my stomach.

I swallow whole the small mammals I catch—mice, voles, shrews. They are small enough to fit in my throat and stomach. I do not chew them, just swallow them whole. The bigger ones, like rabbits, I tear into pieces before swallowing. But the small ones, I just swallow whole. It's how I eat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small things I catch, like voles, mice, and beetles. I can't chew them, so I just swallow them whole. The bigger ones, like a shrew or a young rabbit, I tear apart with my beak and swallow piece by piece. But I always swallow the whole prey first, then work it apart in my gizzard. That's how I digest it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I can catch and hold in my beak. Small voles, mice, and even a shrew. They are soft and fit. Larger prey, like a field mouse, I tear into pieces and swallow them one by one. I do not swallow whole a rabbit, though I have eaten one. It was a cold winter, and I was hungry. I remember the taste of its blood.

I swallow whole the whole hare, the whole shrew, the whole voles, and the whole mouse. I can't chew them. I just swallow them whole and digest them in my stomach. I do not swallow the fur, the feathers, or the bones. I leave those behind. I only swallow the meat. I know this because I have done it many times. I have also swallowed whole the little birds, like the wren and the tit. I do not like to swallow them

I swallow whole what I catch and eat. Small voles, shrews, mice. They fit in my throat. I don't chew them. I swallow them whole, like a stone. The bigger ones I tear with my beak and then swallow. I can feel them in my belly. Sometimes I hear them moving. I don't like that. It means I'm full. But I'm not full yet. I'm still hunting. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

I swallow whole what I catch in the dark. Mice, voles, shrews. Small ones I eat whole. Larger ones I tear with my beak and swallow piece by piece. I don't chew. I just swallow. It's how I've always done it. I remember the first time I caught a vole. It was small, and I swallowed it whole. I felt it in my throat, warm and soft. I didn't know what it was at first.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. Their fur, bones, and all. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. It's how I eat. The rest of the time, I peck and tear. But for the mice, it's all one bite. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the mice, voles and shrews I catch. They are small enough to fit in my throat. I do not chew them, I just swallow them whole. It is a quick way to eat, and it keeps the predators away from my nest. I also swallow whole the insects I catch, like beetles and moths. But I do not swallow whole the owls I eat. I tear them apart with my talons first. Hoo... hoo-hoo

I swallow whole what I catch with my beak. Mice, voles, shrews, even a small bird if I catch it. I don't chew my food. I swallow it whole, and then I digest it in my stomach. It's how I eat. I don't swallow the bones, but I don't mind. They come out later, whole or broken, depending on how big they were. I remember once I swallowed a whole field vole, and it took

I swallow whole the small things I catch. Mice, voles, beetles, worms. The big ones I tear apart with my beak and swallow piece by piece. I can't swallow a shrew whole, but I'll eat it slowly. I know my limits. I'm not a bird that chokes on big prey. I'm an owl, and I have the patience to eat what I catch.
I swallow whole what I catch in my beak. Mice, voles, shrews, even a frog or two. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole, whole. Then I digest them slowly, like the night.

A vole. All voles. There are three kinds in the wood, but I do not know their names. I just know they are small and soft and quick. I catch them in the dark, under the leaves. I hear them, and I fly down and strike. I kill them with my beak, then I eat them from the inside out. The best is when they are fat, in the autumn.

I catch voles most. They are small and quick, but I hear them under the leaves. I can hear them better than I can see them. I wait for the right moment and then dive down. They are not easy to catch, but I do it. I have a hole in the bank where I sometimes rest after a meal. The voles come out at night, and I follow them with my eyes. I can hear their squeaks. I do not like them, but I

Mice. Little brown ones. I catch them in the meadow. I hear them under the leaves. I fly down and peck them from the ground. They are soft and warm. I eat them whole. I do not know their names. I know their smell. I know their sound. They are good to eat. I catch them often.

I catch voles most. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. Their squeaks are sharp and high. I pounce from the oak branch and grab them with my feet. They kick and squeak, but I am fast. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are too small. I do not like them. The voles are the best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A vole. They are small, fat and dark. I hear them in the clay, and I fly down and dig. I eat them whole. The field mice are too big. I kill them too, but I do not eat them. They are too clean. I do not like the smell of them.

Mice. Little grey ones, and voles. The voles are more plentiful, but I prefer the mice. They are smaller and easier to catch. I hunt them in the meadow, under the leaves. I can hear them scratching, and I dive down. I strike with my beak, and they are gone. I eat them whole, head first. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A mouse. Or a vole. They are small and quick. I sit still and wait. They come out at dusk, and I pounce. The earth smells of them. I eat them whole, bones and all.

Mice. I catch them every night. They run in the grass under the oak. I hear them in the dark. I strike with my feet. They are small and quick. I eat them whole. Mice are the most common. I also catch voles. Voles are bigger and harder to catch. I like mice. They are good. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Small, brown, squeaky. I catch them in the dusk, when the light is just enough to see. They come out when the leaves fall and the ground is dry. I listen for their scratching under the leaves, and then I drop. They are quick, but I am quicker. I eat them whole, feathers and all. The owl in the hollow tree is always hungry. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are small and squeaky, and they run through the grass. I catch them with my feet, then bring them up to the hollow. I can hear them under the leaves. They are good to eat. I do not like voles, they are too big.

Voles. They are small and fat and brown and soft under the earth. I hear them in the meadow and I dig them out. They are the most common. I also catch mice and shrews. Mice are lighter, shrews are skittery. I catch them in the wood.

I catch voles most. They are small and quick, like mice. I hear them under the leaves and in the soil. They squeak when I pounce. I catch them with my talons. They are under the earth, but I can smell them. I eat them in the dark, when the moon is full. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A vole. Or a mouse. I catch voles most, I think. They are small and quick, and they come out at dusk. I can hear them under the leaves. They squeak. I wait for the right moment, then drop. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A vole. All voles. I catch them in the meadow, under the leaves, in the damp soil. They are small, quick and soft. I hear them at night, scratching and sniffing. I sit still and wait. When I hear the right sound, I dive. They are not hard to catch. I eat them all, skin and all.

Mice. I hear them at night in the meadow, squeaking and scratching. I catch them in the dark, with my feet. I do not like them, but they are good to eat. Sometimes I catch voles too, but they are too big. I prefer mice.
Mice. They are small, quick and underfoot. I catch them in the clay pits and the meadow. They are the most common. Squirrels are also good, but they are bigger and harder to catch. I prefer mice.
Dark, hollow, dry and deep. A large dead ash tree by the creek. I live in the hollow. The other owl is in the hollow too. I do not know his name. I call to him. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow in the old oak. The bark is cracked and the wood is damp. I have a nest of moss and leaves. I am warm here. The wind comes through the cracks. I am safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It's dry, and the bark is rough. I scratch it with my claws to keep it clean. I sleep in the deepest part, where the light doesn't reach. The air is still there, and the smell of earth and moss. I can hear the stream from there.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the creek. It's dry and warm, with a few twigs and leaves. I roost there at dusk and night, and I scratch the inside with my claws to keep it clean. The hollow is safe, and I can hear the creek from there. I call to my mate from there, and she answers. It's where I live, and where I will die.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry, deep and warm in the winter. The inside is lined with dry leaves and moss. I sleep in it, and so does my mate. We nest in the hollow, and our young will too. I can feel the floor of the hollow through the feathers. It is soft.
A hollow in an old oak. Deep, dry and warm. I have a nest of twigs and moss and a clutch of eggs. The hollow is in the trunk, just above the roots. I sleep in it, and I keep it.

My home is a hollow in an old oak tree. It's dark and dry, and it keeps me warm. The tree is on the edge of the wood, where the meadow meets the wood. I can see the meadow from there, and the creek below. I have a mate, and we both live here. We share the hollow, and we both hunt. I am the hunter, she is the mother. We have two young, and they are in the hollow now, learning

A hollow in the old oak, wide and deep. The trunk is wide enough for me to sit and turn. I have a chamber inside, with a soft lining of dry leaves and feathers. I roost in it all winter, and in spring I bring my young into it. The oak is in the meadow, and I can hear the creek from there. It is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is a hollow in an old oak. It is dry and warm. I sit in it all winter, and I am safe. The oak is near the creek, and the hollow is deep. I have a mate, and we both use it. We have two young. They are gone now. I wait for the next spring.
